procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated August 25, 1969 of the Gujarat High Court at Ahmedabad
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The Inspector of Factories filed a complaint against the Manager of Arun Mills Ltd. The Chief City Magistrate dismissed the complaint, finding the prosecution was barred by time. The Inspector of Factories then filed a revision application before the Gujarat High Court. The High Court set aside the order of the Chief City Magistrate.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Manager of Arun Mills Ltd. appealed to the Supreme Court by Special Leave after the High Court set aside the Magistrate's order.

issue.issue_text: Whether the 'knowledge of the commission of the offence' under Section 106 of the Factories Act, 1948, is acquired on the date of receiving the report of an accident, or on the date when an inquiry reveals all the necessary elements constituting the offence.

facts: An Inspector received a report about an accident where a worker's hand was crushed in a machine.

More than three months after receiving this report, the Inspector conducted an inquiry and discovered that the dangerous parts of the machine were not properly fenced, which constituted an offence under the Factories Act.

A complaint was filed shortly after the inquiry, but the accused argued it was barred by the three-month limitation period under Section 106 of the Act, claiming the period started when the Inspector first received the accident report.
law: Section 106 of the Factories Act, 1948, provides that a complaint must be made within three months of the date on which the 'commission of the offence came to the knowledge of an Inspector'.
application: The Court drew a clear distinction between 'knowledge of an accident' and 'knowledge of the commission of an offence', stating they are not the same thing.

It examined the initial accident report and found that while it described the incident, it did not contain the necessary elements to establish that a specific offence (i.e., that the machinery was not securely fenced) had been committed.

The Court rejected the argument that the limitation period should start from when the Inspector 'ought to have' acquired knowledge had they been more diligent. It held that the statute's plain language refers to the date of *actual* knowledge ('came to the knowledge'), not a hypothetical or constructive date.
The Court emphasized that in interpreting statutes of limitation, it must follow the clear wording of the law, and questions of equity or hardship are irrelevant.
Therefore, the Inspector only gained knowledge of the commission of the offence on the date of the inquiry, when the specific breach of the Act was revealed.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that the 'knowledge of the commission of the offence' under Section 106 is acquired on the date an inquiry reveals all the necessary elements constituting the offence, not on the earlier date of receiving an accident report that does not, by itself, establish that an offence occurred. The limitation period begins from the date of actual knowledge.

issue.issue_text: Whether the starting point for the period of limitation under Section 106 of the Act can be the date on which the Inspector would or ought to have acquired knowledge of the commission of the offence, had he been diligent in making an inquiry.

facts: An accident occurred, and a report was sent to the Inspector.
The Inspector conducted an inquiry several months later and subsequently filed a complaint.

The appellant argued that the prosecution was barred by the limitation period in Section 106 of the Act, which requires a complaint to be filed within three months of the Inspector gaining knowledge of the offence.

The appellant contended that the limitation period should have started earlier, specifically when the Inspector *would have* or *ought to have* known about the offence if he had conducted the inquiry more promptly.
law: Section 106 of the Act states that the limitation period for filing a complaint begins on "the date on which the alleged commission of the offence came to the knowledge of an Inspector."
application: The Court performed a strict and literal interpretation of the statutory language in Section 106.
It held that the phrase "came to the knowledge" refers to the date of the Inspector's *actual* knowledge, not a hypothetical date of constructive knowledge (i.e., when he 'ought to have known').

The Court explicitly rejected the idea of equating "the date on which the alleged offence came to the knowledge of an Inspector" with "the date on which the alleged offence ought to have come to his knowledge," stating that such an interpretation would only be possible in the "jurisprudence of Humpty Dumpty."
It was noted that the statute does not require an inquiry to be conducted within any specific period, which weakened the argument that a delay in inquiry should affect the limitation period.
The Court also distinguished between knowledge of an 'accident' (which the initial report provided) and knowledge of an 'offence' (which was only gained after the inquiry).

Finally, the Court asserted that when interpreting a statute of limitation, principles of equity and hardship, such as the deplorable delay by the Inspector, are irrelevant; the plain text of the law must be followed.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument, concluding that the starting point for the limitation period under Section 106 is the date of the Inspector's actual knowledge of the commission of the offence, not a hypothetical date on which he could or should have acquired that knowledge through more diligent action.

issue.issue_text: Whether questions of equity and hardship are relevant when interpreting a statutory provision that prescribes a period of limitation.

facts: A complaint was filed against the appellant for an offense under the Factories Act, 1948.
The appellant argued that the prosecution was barred by the statute of limitations under Section 106 of the Act.
Section 106 requires a complaint to be made within three months of the date the offense came to the 'knowledge of an Inspector'.
The appellant contended that the Inspector should have known about the offense earlier if they had been diligent in making an inquiry after an accident was reported, and that this delay was unfair.
law: The primary legal principle is that when interpreting a statutory provision that prescribes a period of limitation, questions of equity and hardship are irrelevant.
Section 106 of the Factories Act explicitly makes the 'date of knowledge of the commission of the offence' the starting point for the limitation period.
application: The Court focused on the clear and unambiguous wording of Section 106.
It rejected the argument that the starting point for the limitation period should be the date on which the Inspector 'would or ought to have acquired knowledge' of the offense.
The Court stated that equating the actual 'date of knowledge' with a hypothetical date of when knowledge should have been acquired is an incorrect reading of the law.

It reasoned that since the statute does not mandate a specific timeframe for an inquiry, any delay in conducting one, however 'deplorable', cannot change the starting point of limitation defined in the statute.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that it must adhere to the clear wording of the statute. Therefore, arguments based on equity or hardship, such as the Inspector's delay in discovering the offense, are 'out of place' and cannot be used to alter the statutory starting point for the limitation period, which is the date of actual knowledge.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the 'knowledge of the commission of the offence' under Section 106 of the Factories Act, 1948, is acquired on the date of receiving the report of an accident, or on the date when an inquiry reveals all the necessary elements constituting the offence.
appellant_arguments: The appellant argued that the prosecution was barred by time because the Inspector came to know about the commission of the offence on the date the accident report was received by him.
The appellant contended that the facts mentioned in the report were sufficient to convey the knowledge of the commission of an offence.
respondent_arguments: The respondent (the State) argued that the Inspector did not get any knowledge of the commission of an offence from the report.

The respondent contended that the report only indicated an accident had occurred but did not state that the dangerous parts of the machinery were not securely fenced, which is a necessary element of the offence under Section 21(1)(iv)(c).
The respondent argued that knowledge of the commission of the offence was only acquired on the date of the inquiry, and the complaint was filed within three months of that date.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the starting point for the period of limitation under Section 106 of the Act can be the date on which the Inspector would or ought to have acquired knowledge of the commission of the offence, had he been diligent in making an inquiry.
appellant_arguments: The appellant argued that when the report conveyed information about the accident, the Inspector should have enquired into it with reasonable promptness, implying that the limitation period should not be extended by the Inspector's delay.
respondent_arguments: The respondent's position, based on the text, is that the statutory trigger for the limitation period is the date of actual knowledge ('came to the knowledge of an Inspector'), not a hypothetical date based on when an inquiry should have been conducted.

arguments.issue_text: Whether questions of equity and hardship are relevant when interpreting a statutory provision that prescribes a period of limitation.
appellant_arguments: The appellant's argument that the Inspector should have acted with 'reasonable promptness' implies an appeal to fairness, suggesting it is inequitable for the accused to be disadvantaged by the Inspector's delay in launching an inquiry.
respondent_arguments: The respondent's argument relies on a strict interpretation of the statutory language, implying that the plain text of the limitation provision must be applied without considering external factors like equity or hardship to the accused.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: For a statute of limitations where the starting point is the "date on which the alleged offence came to the knowledge of an Inspector," the period begins from the date of actual knowledge of the commission of the offense, not from a date on which the Inspector would or ought to have acquired such knowledge had they been diligent.
obiter: In interpreting a provision in a statute prescribing a period of limitation for instituting a proceeding, questions of equity and hardship are out of place.
Knowledge of an accident is not the same as knowledge of the commission of an offence.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: Knowledge of the commission of an offence under Section 106 of the Factories Act is not acquired from a mere report of an accident. Such knowledge is only gained when the Inspector becomes aware of all the necessary elements that constitute the specific offence. In this case, the accident report did not reveal that the dangerous machinery was not securely fenced as required by Section 21(1)(iv)(c), and therefore, the Inspector only acquired knowledge of the offence upon conducting an inquiry, which became the starting point for the limitation period.
legal_tests_applied: To determine if 'knowledge of the commission of the offence' has been acquired, the information received must be assessed to see if it reveals all the necessary elements that go to constitute the offence in question.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant's argument that the accident report was sufficient to convey knowledge of the offence failed because the report did not contain the necessary elements of an offence under Section 21(1)(iv)(c). Specifically, the report did not state that the dangerous parts of the machinery were not securely fenced or otherwise safe by position or construction.

The court rejected the argument that the limitation period should start from when the Inspector 'ought to have acquired knowledge' had he been diligent. The court found it difficult to read such a requirement into Section 106, as the statute explicitly makes the 'date of knowledge' the starting point and does not mandate a specific timeframe for an inquiry.

The appellant's implied argument based on the hardship caused by the Inspector's delay was dismissed, as the court held that 'questions of equity and hardship are out of place' when interpreting a statutory provision that prescribes a period of limitation.
why_respondent_won: The respondent successfully argued that the accident report only conveyed knowledge of an accident, not an offence. The court agreed, finding that the report lacked the specific details required to establish a violation of Section 21(1)(iv)(c), and that the Inspector only gained knowledge of the commission of the offence on the date of his inquiry.

The respondent's position that the limitation period is triggered by the date of actual knowledge was upheld. The court's reasoning was based on a plain reading of Section 106, which makes the 'date of knowledge of the commission of the offence the starting point of the period of limitation.'
policy_considerations: In interpreting a provision in a statute prescribing a period of limitation for instituting a proceeding, questions of equity and hardship are out of place.

The court will not read a requirement for a diligent or prompt inquiry into a statute where the legislature has not provided for one, especially when setting the starting point for a limitation period.
